title: What do the OCC heightened standards require for talent management and director training?
description: OCC heightened standards, 12 CFR Part 30 Appendix D: talent management, director training and the pending $700 billion threshold, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) heightened standards, 12 CFR Part 30 Appendix D, apply to insured national banks, federal savings associations and federal branches with average total consolidated assets of $50 billion or more. Paragraph II.L requires talent development, recruitment and succession processes so people who make or influence material risk decisions have the necessary knowledge, skills and abilities. Paragraph III.E requires a formal, ongoing training program for all directors.
keyTakeaways: Appendix D applies to covered banks with average total consolidated assets of $50 billion or more, and to smaller banks whose parent controls at least one covered bank. An OCC proposal of December 30, 2025 would raise the threshold to $700 billion; as at November 2026 it has not been finalized.

Paragraph II.L requires processes for talent development, recruitment and succession planning covering management and employees responsible for or influencing material risk decisions, plus a board-approved written talent management program.
Front line units, independent risk management and internal audit must each develop, attract and retain talent, maintain adequate staffing, and follow II.L talent management processes.
Paragraph III.E requires the board to establish and adhere to a formal, ongoing training program for all directors, considering their knowledge and experience and the bank's risk profile.
A final rule published April 10, 2026 (91 FR 18279) removed reputation risk from the Appendix D risk categories, effective June 9, 2026.
regulator: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
appliesTo: Insured national banks, insured federal savings associations and insured federal branches of foreign banks with average total consolidated assets of $50 billion or more
Insured banks under $50 billion whose parent company controls at least one covered bank
Boards of directors of covered banks (director training, talent program approval, annual self-assessment)
Front line units, independent risk management and internal audit, and the employees who are responsible for or influence material risk decisions

sections.heading: Which banks do the OCC heightened standards apply to?

blocks.text: The guidelines apply to covered banks: any insured national bank, insured federal savings association or insured federal branch of a foreign bank with average total consolidated assets equal to or greater than $50 billion, plus any smaller such bank whose parent company controls at least one covered bank. Average total consolidated assets are measured over the four most recent consecutive quarters of Call Report data. The text is at [12 CFR Part 30, Appendix D](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/12/appendix-D_to_part_30), issued under section 39 of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act.

blocks.title: Threshold change pending as at November 2026
blocks.text: On December 30, 2025 the OCC published a [proposal](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/12/30/2025-23986/occ-guidelines-establishing-heightened-standards-for-certain-large-insured-national-banks-insured) (90 FR 61084) to raise the threshold for applying the guidelines from $50 billion to $700 billion and to clarify certain compliance dates. The comment period closed March 2, 2026. As at November 2026 no final rule has been published and the codified threshold remains $50 billion. Banks between the two thresholds should track the outcome before reducing any program.

The original compliance dates ran from November 10, 2014, phased by size: banks of $750 billion or more complied on that date, banks of $100 billion to $750 billion within six months, and banks of $50 billion to $100 billion within 18 months. A bank that later crosses $50 billion should comply within 18 months of the as-of date of the most recent Call Report used to calculate its average.

sections.heading: What does paragraph II.L require for talent management?

blocks.text: Paragraph II.L ties workforce capability directly to risk governance. It reads:

blocks.title: 12 CFR Part 30, Appendix D, paragraph II.L
blocks.text: "A covered bank should establish and adhere to processes for talent development, recruitment, and succession planning to ensure that management and employees who are responsible for or influence material risk decisions have the knowledge, skills, and abilities to effectively identify, measure, monitor, and control relevant risks."

The board of directors, or an appropriate board committee, has three specific duties under II.L. It should appoint a Chief Executive Officer and appoint or approve a Chief Audit Executive and one or more Chief Risk Executives with the skills and abilities for their roles. It should review and approve a written talent management program covering development, recruitment and succession planning for those individuals, their direct reports and other potential successors. And it should require management to assign specific responsibilities within the program and hold those individuals accountable for its effectiveness.

The phrase "responsible for or influence material risk decisions" is the key scoping test. It reaches beyond executives to anyone whose judgment shapes material risk, which in practice means a population the bank must define and keep current. A [competency framework](/glossary/competency-framework) for those roles is the usual way to make "knowledge, skills, and abilities" assessable.

sections.heading: What talent duties apply to front line units, risk management and internal audit?

blocks.text: Each of the three lines carries the same two talent duties. Front line units under II.C.1(e) and (f), independent risk management under II.C.2(g) and (h), and internal audit under II.C.3(g) and (h) should each develop, attract and retain talent and maintain staffing levels required to carry out their role effectively, and establish and adhere to talent management processes that comply with II.L.

Paragraph II.M links pay to the same goal: compensation and performance management programs should be appropriate to attract and retain the talent needed to design, implement and maintain an effective risk governance framework. Together these provisions mean the OCC can examine a covered bank's training, hiring and succession records as evidence that each line is capable of doing what the risk governance framework says it does.

sections.heading: What training must directors of a covered bank receive?

blocks.text: Paragraph III.E requires the board to establish and adhere to a formal, ongoing training program for all directors. The program should consider the directors' knowledge and experience and the covered bank's risk profile, and should include, as appropriate, training on complex products, services, lines of business and risks with a significant impact on the bank; laws, regulations and supervisory requirements applicable to the bank; and other topics identified by the board.

Paragraph III.F adds an annual board self-assessment that evaluates the board's effectiveness in meeting the Section III standards. The self-assessment is a natural input to the next year's director training plan. For reporting conventions, see [how to report training compliance to the board](/guides/how-to-report-training-compliance-to-the-board).

sections.heading: Does Appendix D require training for all employees?

blocks.text: Not in those words, but paragraph II.G.2 comes close. It requires the risk governance framework to provide for initial communication and ongoing reinforcement of the risk appetite statement throughout the covered bank "in a manner that causes all employees to align their risk-taking decisions with applicable aspects of the risk appetite statement."

Communication that causes alignment is an outcome standard. A bank that only publishes the risk appetite statement on its intranet will find it hard to show that employees' decisions align with it. Role-specific training on the applicable limits and escalation routes, with some check of understanding, is the more defensible approach. Since June 9, 2026, the risk categories in paragraph II.B are credit, interest rate, liquidity, price, operational, compliance and strategic risk; reputation risk was removed by the [final rule on reputation risk](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/04/10/2026-06947/prohibition-on-the-use-of-reputation-risk-by-regulators) (91 FR 18279, amending Appendix D at 91 FR 18293), so training content that still lists it should be updated.

sections.heading: What happens if a covered bank does not meet the guidelines?

blocks.text: The OCC can require a compliance plan. Under 12 CFR 30.3, if the OCC determines a bank has failed to satisfy a safety and soundness standard set by guideline, it may request a compliance plan by letter or through a report of examination. Under [12 CFR 30.4](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/12/30.4), the bank must file the plan within 30 days unless the OCC sets a different period, describing the steps it will take and the timeline.

If a bank fails to submit an acceptable plan or fails in any material respect to implement it, 30.4(d) requires the OCC to order correction of the deficiency, and 12 CFR 30.6 allows judicial enforcement and civil money penalties for failure to comply with a final order. A talent or director training gap is therefore not merely a supervisory comment: it can enter a formal process with fixed deadlines.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry defines the knowledge, skills and abilities expected of each role that makes or influences material risk decisions before training is built, and links each requirement to the risk categories and limits it supports. That gives the board and examiners a traceable line from Appendix D to role definitions to training and assessment evidence. See the [financial services](/industries/financial-services) page.

faqs.q: Are the OCC heightened standards regulations or guidelines?
faqs.a: They are guidelines issued under section 39 of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act and codified as Appendix D to 12 CFR Part 30. Failure to meet them can lead the OCC to request a compliance plan under 12 CFR 30.3, with an order and enforcement available if the bank fails to submit or implement an acceptable plan.

faqs.q: Does Appendix D set a number of training hours for directors?
faqs.a: No. Paragraph III.E requires a formal, ongoing training program for all directors that considers their knowledge, experience and the bank's risk profile. It names topics but sets no hours or fixed frequency.

faqs.q: Will the heightened standards stop applying to banks under $700 billion?
faqs.a: Only if the OCC finalizes its December 30, 2025 proposal (90 FR 61084). As at November 2026 the codified threshold remains $50 billion. Covered banks in the affected range should maintain their programs until a final rule is published and takes effect.

faqs.q: Can a covered bank use its parent company's framework?
faqs.a: Yes, in part. Paragraph I.3 lets a covered bank use the parent's risk governance framework in its entirety if it meets the minimum standards and the risk profiles are substantially the same, as shown by a documented assessment. Otherwise the bank may rely on parent components in consultation with the OCC.

factCheck.claim: Appendix D applies to insured national banks, FSAs and federal branches with average total consolidated assets of $50 billion or more, and to smaller banks whose parent controls at least one covered bank.

Paragraph II.L requires processes for talent development, recruitment and succession planning for management and employees responsible for or influencing material risk decisions, and a board-reviewed and approved written talent management program.

Paragraph III.E requires a formal, ongoing training program for all directors covering complex products and risks, applicable laws and supervisory requirements, and board-identified topics; III.F requires an annual board self-assessment.
Paragraph II.G.2 requires communication and ongoing reinforcement of the risk appetite statement in a manner that causes all employees to align their risk-taking decisions with it.
Compliance dates were phased from November 10, 2014 ($750 billion or more on that date; $100 to $750 billion within six months; $50 to $100 billion within 18 months).

The OCC proposed on December 30, 2025 (90 FR 61084) to raise the Appendix D threshold from $50 billion to $700 billion; comments closed March 2, 2026. No final rule appears in the Federal Register through November 2026 and the eCFR text still states $50 billion.
The reputation risk final rule (91 FR 18279, April 10, 2026, effective June 9, 2026) amended Appendix D at 91 FR 18293, removing reputation risk from the II.B risk categories.
12 CFR 30.4 requires a compliance plan to be filed within 30 days of an OCC request unless the OCC sets a different period.
